newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela severance deal imperils fiscal balance.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela severance deal imperils fiscal balance.

text.p: Venezuela's fragile fiscal balance could drop sharply into the red on steep interest payments required in an historic agreement signed last week to reform the country's severance pay system, analysts said.
The agreement still has to pass Congressional muster, and its passage will require the probably time-consuming reform of supporting legislation.

But the quirky new scheme puts the government's feet to the fire in a way the current system doesn't. Venezuela's "prestaciones," literally "borrowings," function as a severance-pension package, against which workers can also borrow to buy homes or go to school.
Each month, the funds will accrue interest, acting as a nest egg as well.

The new scheme is different in that the government must set aside a certain amount of cash every month for each of its 1.3 million public sector workers, instead of eternally postponing the payouts as it has under the current system. Venezuelans consider the prestaciones close to a birthright.
But once passed into law, it will shoot government spending up by some 12 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) over the next five years, analysts warn.

"If the agreement is put in place without the government having in hand a stable revenue stream, the fiscal deficit could reach four percent of GDP annually over the coming years, basically due to interest payments," said one economist linked to the government, who asked to remain anonymous.
That figure is in stark contrast to the small surplus hoped for this year.

The government is still squaring its accounts on the deal -- signed by government, union and private sector leaders Monday last week -- under which Venezuela will move towards a new, fully funded, severance pay system.

First, however, past liabilities have to be met. Preliminary official calculations suggest the government's total liability will reach 4.8 trillion bolivars ($10 billion) on the build-up of unpaid outlays to workers.

To dig out from under past-due payments, the government agreed to pay its workers -- over a five-year period -- one month's pay per each year worked up to a limit of 11 years, plus a special bonus of up to 200,000 bolivars ($419) for each year worked, also up to an 11-year limit.

The interest payments alone on the arrears -- set as the average of lending and borrowing rates at Venezuela's six largest commercial banks -- will annually cost, at current rates of interest, some 1.2 trillion bolivars ($2.5 billion), the economist said.
According to recent Central Bank figures, the average lending rate in the first week of March was 17.64 percent while the average short-term deposit rate was 7.00 percent.
Under the new system, employees will receive 45 days' pay for the first year worked, and then 60 days of pay for each subsequent year.

With such payments looming, analysts say Venezuela is unlikely to approach the 0.9 percent of GDP fiscal surplus it enjoyed in 1996 on a one-off 40 percent devaluation of the bolivar that saw local currency revenues leap on soaring dollar-denominated oil prices.

Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar has said the government will meet the payments with an issue of up to 600 billion bolivars ($1.2 billion) of paper, cut public investment, and use some of the revenues from telephone CANTV's $1 billion privatization last year.
But, "Venezuela's debt profile is rising in a permanent way and could give rise to a chronic fiscal deficit," said another economist with access to union and government figures.
Previous fiscal forecasts for the year had foreseen a 0.8 percent of GDP surplus, revised down from 3.5 percent after the public sector received a 75 percent average wage increase in February.

One alternative would be to accelerate the so-far stalled privatization of iron and aluminum companies held by the para- statal Corporacion Venezolana de Guayana (CVG) that could bring between $2-3 billion, the economist said.
A further option, he added, could also include a share issue by state-owned oil company PdVSA, hitherto a Venezuelan taboo.
((-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
